In watch collecting it's often said that you can't wear the box.  However, in the 1960s and early '70s the various Enicar distributors around the world put out some retail packaging that was as cutting edge as the watches they held.  Case in point is this Japanese domestic market jewel box from the 1960s, which is a perfect backdrop for this MK1B Graph which also came from an estate in Japan.  I've seen these boxes sell for more than I've paid for entire watches, but I have to admit they are pretty cool.

Like the Boeing 707, the Enicar Jet was in its heyday in the mid 1960s.  From what I have seen over the years, this configuration is one of Enicar's more popular iterations of the Super Jet: black 'T Swiss' dial with large painted Saturn logo, tuning fork hands, lollipop sweeper, paint-tipped GMT hand, red font date wheel and thick crowns. Everything you need in a clean, crisp watertight stainless steel package. 

This example sitting atop a 'torre pendente' di EPSA was worn in period by a US Navy serviceman and has a case dated 8/65 with a serial number of 727xxx.

More weekend Enicar Jet minutiae:  Another early Super Jet variant with some interesting details.  Note the small printed Saturn logo and absence of the T for tritium on the dial, but with the black font / closed-jaw number date disk as was used in the '33' variants.

This example has a case  date of 10/64 and a 677XXX case number.  I have seen other 10/64 case Super Jets in the 678XXX range with 'T Swiss' dials, large Saturn and red font / open-jaw dates.  I don't know how many were produced with the details shown here, but it doesn't really matter, as to me it's just a great vintage watch with cool period details.  Enicar seems to have had many running changes among their modular parts, so there's a bit of variety in the configuration of these, especially in the early pieces. 

Thank you to vintage1688 for letting this one join my fleet some years ago.

Coffee in hand, I'm taking a Sunday deep dive into Enicar's 33-jewel GMT diver from the 1960s:  Paddle hands and several superfluous jewels set this Singapore-sold early SuperJet 33 apart from non-33 variants marketed outside of Asia. 

A number of other details also distinguish the 33 Jewel models from standard versions sold in the Rest of the World: applied Saturn logos on the dials, unique 24 hour bezels in mirrored silver and black, non-lollipop second hands, black font on the date wheel with closed-jaw '6' and '9' numerals and  the earliest versions of the Jet 33 have the crescent GMT hand in red vs. the red-tipped straight hand seen on the Super Jet 33 and non-33 models.  Most 33s do not appear to have dated case backs, but production was likely from '64 in to '65.

Some 60-odd years on, that EPSA technology is still more than up to the intended task. And it still looks great doing it.

While looking through some watch paperwork recently  noticed it was fifty-five years ago today that a Mr. Armijo of Los Angeles spent $120 in 1969 cash for the purchase of this Favre-Leuba Sea Sky on a leather strap. 

A consumer in 1969 with $120 to spend on a chronograph had many choices and I have to wonder why the less-common Favre-Leuba was his choice.  The countdown dive bezel?  Did he really need a Telemeter?  Maybe a 45 MPH tachy?  I will probably never know, but I appreciate a watch with history, especially when there's a local connection.
